analysis.one_liner: Eases federal regulations on banks and trims some consumer credit disclosure and liability rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in a House Banking subcommittee from August 1995 until the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have loosened federal rules for banks and other lenders in several ways: well-capitalized, well-run banking companies could buy other banks without prior government approval, ATMs would no longer count as bank branches needing approval, small banks would get less frequent examinations, and lenders would get broad protection from liability — including liability for pollution on property they finance and liability for errors in consumer credit disclosures. It would also have trimmed consumer protections in the Truth in Lending Act, such as the right to cancel certain refinanced home loans, while adding a few new consumer disclosures, most notably requiring ATMs to post their fees at the machine.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, savings institutions, mortgage lenders, and loan servicers gain the most: fewer prior-approval requirements for mergers and branches, lighter examination schedules for small banks, caps on damages for mortgage disclosure errors, exemptions from the right to cancel certain refinancings, and protection from environmental liability on loans gone bad. Consumers get a few narrow gains, like fee disclosures posted at ATMs and clearer disclosures on car and equipment leases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks, mortgage lenders, and loan servicers

how_it_helps.text: Well-capitalized, well-managed bank holding companies could acquire other banks or nonbank companies without prior Federal Reserve approval, with only advance notice instead [S2].
Small depository institutions with up to $250 million in assets (raised from $175 million) would be examined on site every 18 months instead of annually, cutting compliance costs [S2].
ATMs and remote service units would be exempted from the definition of a bank branch, sparing banks approval and closure-notification requirements for them [S2].
Consumers would gain a new right to know: any operator of an electronic terminal, including ATMs, would have to disclose the fee it charges at the time the service is provided [S2].
Consumer lease disclosures would be expanded to include the capitalized cost, residual value, and end-of-lease purchase price, so shoppers can compare lease deals [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Borrowers and consumers bear the cost in weakened protections: tighter limits on suing lenders over faulty Truth in Lending disclosures, loss of the right to cancel certain refinanced mortgages, exemption from liability for some lenders of pollution on foreclosed property, and less federal oversight of mergers, branch openings, and branch closings in local communities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Borrowers and communities near affected banks

drawbacks.text: The bill caps damages at $250 to $2,500 per individual mortgage-secured credit violation under the Truth in Lending Act and shields creditors and debt buyers (assignees) from liability unless a disclosure error is apparent on the face of the statement, making it harder to penalize inaccurate cost disclosures [S2].
It denies borrowers the right to rescind certain refinancings of residential mortgages, a remedy that otherwise lets homeowners undo loans with disclosure violations [S2].

Lenders that test themselves for discrimination by sending in fake applicants would no longer have to turn those results over to fair-lending or fair-housing enforcers, limiting the evidence available in discrimination cases [S2].

Lenders would be shielded from federal environmental liability unless they actually participated in managing the polluting activity, shifting cleanup risk for contaminated collateral away from banks [S2].

Exempting ATMs and merged or nearby branches from closure-notice requirements, applied retroactively to 1991, would reduce the public notice communities currently get when local banking access disappears [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Streamlining overlapping bank rules and adding ATM fee and lease-cost disclosures had real value, but the bill paid for bank relief by trimming consumer rights in exactly the areas — mortgage disclosure accuracy, rescission, lender liability, and fair-lending evidence — where enforcement was weakest. For ordinary borrowers the trade tilted toward the industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Banking Committee and then to its financial institutions subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no hearing, no vote, nothing.

narrative.text: Rep. Bruce Vento (D-MN) introduced the bill on August 1, 1995, joined by eight other House Democrats as original cosponsors [S1].
The House referred it to the Committee on Banking and Financial Services on the day of introduction [S1].
On August 11, 1995, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, and no further action appears in the record [S1].
The bill had 9 cosponsors, all Democrats [S4].
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill died without ever coming to a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and mortgage lenders are worse off than they would have been under the bill, while borrowers keep the existing Truth in Lending protections — disclosure tolerances, rescission rights, and liability rules — that the bill would have loosened. Nothing changed for anyone.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Borrowers who kept existing credit protections

sides.party_line_note: All ten original sponsors were Democrats, and the bill never advanced far enough for any roll-call; the Republican-run committee simply never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have cut prior-approval requirements for mergers, branches, and divestitures for well-capitalized institutions and reduced examination frequency for smaller banks. Some relief (ATM fee disclosure duties, outside-director mandates) cuts the other way, and the largest banks would have gained the most from streamlined acquisitions.

It would have excluded many closing fees from the finance charge calculation, narrowed rescission rights, capped damages at $250–$2,500, and limited assignee and servicer liability under the Truth in Lending Act. Those changes would have reduced lenders' exposure to borrower lawsuits at borrowers' expense.

industries.industry: Commercial lenders exposed to environmental cleanup costs
industries.note: The lender-liability title would have protected lenders from federal environmental liability unless they actually managed the polluting activity, moving cleanup risk off lenders' balance sheets and onto other parties, including any public cleanup funds.

industries.industry: Outside law firms and accounting firms serving large banks
industries.note: The bill would have barred outside counsel and accountants from sitting on the boards of depository institutions with more than $250 million in assets, costing those firms board seats. It targets conflicts of interest between a bank's advisers and its governance.
